"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold."

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

"There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption."

Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain."

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day."

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. "

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

Want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras, lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

#802. Anne Hathaway Gives Birth, Welcomes Baby No. 3 With Adam Shulman

Anne Hathaway gave birth to her and husband Adam Shulman's third baby together, according to multiple outlets. The couple—who married in 2012—are already parents to sons Jonathan, 10, and Jack, 6.

Anne Hathaway has some news that will thrill you.

The Devil Wears Prada star gave birth to her third child with husband Adam Shulman, according to multiple outlets, with TMZ sharing photos of the actress walking around New York City with the newborn.

While Hathaway or Shulman—already parents to sons Jonathan, 10, and Jack, 6—haven't spoken publicly about welcoming their newest little one, they are more than prepared to take on their new roles as parents of three.

"The thing that to remember about boys is they have feelings," Hathaway—who tied the knot with Shulman in 2012—told Access Hollywood in July. "Sometimes, we think about that more in the realm of girls, but it's just as important to give boys that emotional foundation and make sure they feel just as safe as as we make our girls feel."

The Oscar winner first announced her pregnancy in June, sharing a video set to "Baby, I'm Yours" by Barbara Lewis in which she was seen cradling her growing baby bump in a flowing white dress.

She continued to bare her belly during the press tour for The Odyssey, most notably wearing a red, long-sleeved peplum jumpsuit by Ashlyn New York backwards by mistake.

"I did?" Hathaway quipped in a July 1 TikTok, after man fans pointed out that the one-piece looked different on the model who wore the jumpsuit during the label's Spring/Summer 2026 fashion show. "I did. I did."

But in Hathaway's defense, she's not the first pregnant star to tweak an outfit around her baby belly.

"I've heard from other pregnant women that the maternity hack is if you have to go to an event, you get a dress that has a train," she explained to Access Hollywood later that month, "and then you wear the train backwards and the train accommodates for the bump."

Plus, the Princess Diaries alum considered her baby bump to be the best fashion accessory. As she told E! News at the New York premiere of The Odyssey on July 14, "Cannot be beat."

"This is a lovely microphone,” Hathaway said while cradling her belly on the red carpet, “but I prefer my accessory.”

Besides, her pregnancy was an overall lovely surprise.

"It’s amazing," Hathway shared during a July 14 appearance on Late Night with Seth Meyers, before joking that she and Shulman—who she married in 2012—"knew what we were doing, but we were so shocked it worked."

"We were so shocked it went this way," she continued, "so we’re calling this one our buzzer-beater.”

Read on for more insight into Hathaway's motherhood journey, in her own words.

Anne Hathaway shared the special and exciting news that she and her hubby are having another baby! "It's not for a movie...⁣⁣#2," she wrote on Instagram, showing off her bump. "All kidding aside, for everyone going through infertility and conception hell, please know it was not a straight line to either of my pregnancies. Sending you extra love."

"They get down on the child's level and speak to them eye-to-eye to make their child feel empowered," she told The Sunday Times. "I thought that was really cool. I started doing that with Jonathan."

"I hadn't planned on ever confirming it and then I just, I had seen a photographer while I was on vacation, taking a photo, and I just thought, 'It's such a joyful and a sacred experience, you know, carrying life,'" Hathaway explained to E! News. "And I just thought, 'I don't want the first version of this to be out there with me covering or scowling at someone.'"

She told E! News that getting sleep has been challenging. "Honestly, I haven't slept in eight weeks. I have no idea what I'm saying," the actress jokingly stated. "This is probably going to go down as not the most normal interview on E! News."

"I'm going to stop drinking while my son is in my house just because I don't totally love the way I do it," Hathaway admitted to Ellen DeGeneres on her talk show. "He's getting to an age where he really does need me all the time in the mornings. I did one school run one day where I dropped him off at school, I wasn't driving, but I was hungover, and that was enough for me. I didn't love that one."

"The kind of mother I'll be depends on the kind of children I have," the Ocean's 8 actress shared with Vogue about the ultimate role she has as a mother.

"I can't believe we don't already have it," she shared with Elle magazine, further explaining that "We're encouraged to judge each other, but we should be turning our focus to the people and institutions who should be supporting us and currently aren't."

"I'm not perfect, but if I'm frustrated or distracted, I'm good at making sure he's safe and walking away, calming down and then coming back to him," she explained to The Sunday Times. She said "telling that harsh voice to be quiet" is one hard about motherhood. "I fall short every day, but I'm not going to beat myself up about it, I'm going to learn from it."

"I'm sorry. I am a new mother and I didn't time the feeding schedule—well, like I have any control over it," Hathaway said on Good Morning America with a laugh as she does press for the Alice Through the Looking Glass. "My kid was hungry, I had to feed him, I missed the first 20 minutes so I can't tell you about the beginning of the movie."

"When [my son] Johnny was a week old and I was holding him and I was in the ninth level of ecstasy, I just all of a sudden thought, 'Mommy guilt is invented nonsense,'" she told Elle magazine.

#801. ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future

At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’

After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.

“What I’ve seen over the last few years is that I attend meetings where we talk about everything except for the game,” Molango says. “And I think we’ve allowed people to enter the game that did not enter it for the right reasons. They did not enter the game to make it better. They did not enter the game because they loved it. They entered the game because they saw money in the game and because they saw influence in the game. And I’m very concerned about that because, ultimately, if you don’t have a good game, if you don’t have a good product, you don’t have an industry.”

Molango is speaking at a potentially critical juncture for the future of football. Wednesday is the deadline for candidates for the role of Fifa president to put their name forward for March’s election. Gianni Infantino appears likely to win an unprecedented fourth term despite the cascade of scandal that has dogged much of his decade in charge. Infantino’s tenure has also brought about enormous changes of which Molango, whose union had 345 members playing at this year’s World Cup, 27.6% of the total, is highly critical.

The expansion of the World Cup is one central issue; where 32 teams became 48 at the men’s tournament this past summer and perhaps 64 in 2030. The changes, which players’ unions say were made without consulting players, have led to knock-on effects on the calendar that mean the PFA is pursuing Fifa through the European courts to ensure “the legal rights of players to take guaranteed and protected breaks”. But they have also damaged, in Molango’s mind, what should be the sport’s most precious event and for spurious reasons.

“Can anyone who really believes in the concept of the World Cup think that having a 64-team tournament makes sense?” he says. “We may as well call it a summer friendly tournament. And I cannot buy the narrative that says: ‘Oh, it’s about making football truly global.’ That’s just not true. I think it’s disrespectful to think that people in the Congo want to be gifted access to the World Cup. We don’t need favours, we just need opportunities. We want to deserve to be at the World Cup, we don’t need it to be gifted to us, thank you very much. Don’t treat us as if we need to thank you for giving us something.”

Then there is the question of integrity. Last summer’s World Cup brought an incident which, for many in the game, crossed a red line: the overturning of the suspension awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun, after an intervention by Donald Trump. “What happened with Balogun is scandalous,” Molango says. “Because my son can say to me: ‘Football is corrupt.’ It’s unacceptable that you’ve allowed a situation where people can think that. Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.”

Molango was born in Switzerland to a Congolese father and an Italian mother. He is an Italian national and began his career as a professional footballer in Spain, at Atlético Madrid. He made no appearances for the club, however, before moving to Brighton (a club that was a different proposition in 2005: “We were playing at the Withdean and I was washing my own kit at home”). From there he moved across and down the English football pyramid before finishing in Spain. After retirement he retrained in Spain as a lawyer, establishing the country’s first sports law practice, before he became the chief executive of Mallorca. He took the club to the depths of the third tier, then back to La Liga in consecutive seasons before taking charge at the PFA, replacing the longtime leader Gordon Taylor at a time of tumult for the organisation.

To visit the PFA’s smart, new offices in London’s Liverpool Street, bedecked in replica kits and with a timeline of players’ developing rights in the entrance hall, is to see an organisation that has come out the other end of an intensive period of reform. An independent review into the PFA’s governance was launched in 2018 after concerns over the use of funds. The outcome led not only to Molango’s appointment but also to the introduction of a players’ board – now led by the impressive Omar Beckles alongside Ben Davies of Tottenham and Chelsea’s Lucy Bronze among others – as well as non-executive directors and a committee focusing on the ethics of the organisation.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The PFA had a credibility issue,” Molango says. “We called an independent expert. They came in, they assessed, and they changed the governance. So I think we led the way. We demonstrated that sometimes you don’t need to be rotten to be wanting to change, you just need to acknowledge that things move on.”

Ten years after the reforms that followed the Sepp Blatter era, Molango believes that Fifa must change again. “It’s a sick system,” he says, “and for me we shouldn’t be talking about individuals, we should be talking about governance. The system as currently constructed is a system that will always foster the wrong behaviour. Because inevitably the decision taken will not be for what’s good for the game. It will be for what’s good for the next election.”

If change doesn’t occur, there is no guarantee in Molango’s mind that football’s status as the world’s favourite sport, and a cultural unifier, will continue. “I think we live in a world where there’s tough competition for entertainment and what I think will happen is that people will lose interest and move on. They move on to other sports, to other sources of entertainment and in the end we’ll kill the industry. We’ll kill it because we’re no longer the only players in the playground. There’s a lot of people and a lot of people who have a good product. I think we need to go back to focusing on the quality of our product. Because football has a real problem.”

#800. Belief and bench steer Northern Ireland into Nations League top tier

Highlights: Northern Ireland secure to promotion to League A

After going 500 minutes without conceding a goal, Northern Ireland could be forgiven for having to make adjustments to play from behind.

Having travelled to Budapest knowing a point against Hungary would be enough to top Nations League B2, Barnabas Varga's strike after 35 minutes for the hosts at the Puskas Arena altered the picture and, for the first time in the campaign, left Michael O'Neill's side having to chase a game.

Their response to the deficit - on the pitch, from the bench and high in the stands where their suspended manager was watching the game - displayed the best characteristics of a side who had not won at this level before this unbeaten campaign.

While the point from a 1-1 draw in Budapest will be long remembered for Justin Devenny's brilliant equaliser and the scenes of celebration that greeted promotion to the competition's top tier for the first time, it was beyond the highlights and headlines that O'Neill saw the emerging qualities of his side.

"We went behind tonight and it was difficult, you know? Big stadium, big atmosphere, but we came out and played well in the second half and got what we needed from the game," said the manager.

"Those are things that I'm very pleased that are in this squad at such a young age. The technical side of the game we'll always look to improve on, but in terms of the physical, the tactical and the mental side of a game, we're very far ahead of where I thought we would be at this time."

Northern Ireland draw with Hungary to seal Nations League promotion

Watch: Devenny the hero as NI earn promotion

Hungary enjoyed more than 70% possession in the first half, and they could have been further than a goal ahead with Liverpool star Dominik Szoboszlai striking the base of the post after only five minutes.

O'Neill made his first change at half-time, bringing on veteran striker Josh Magennis, while Kieran Morrison, Brodie Spencer and Paul Smyth all followed in the second half.

Magennis and Morrison made a real impact before the equaliser, but it was the belief shown by all involved that O'Neill felt was key to the turnaround.

"I felt in the first half from where I was seeing the game, we just looked a little bit leggy which is natural," added O'Neill.

"I just felt we needed that freshness at the right points in the game that helped us, but it was the belief that we could get back into the game, and the belief that we could see the game out.

"I think we showed a lot of attributes that are in this squad at this moment in time and certainly in the second half that was that was the case."

'I genuinely believe it will only get better' - O'Neill

For all the plaudits earned by this team who conceded just one goal in six games while picking up 12 points, among the most impressive aspects of the campaign has been who they have had to do without.

Talismanic Liverpool defender Conor Bradley has not played for this side in over 12 months through injury.

Ali McCann is another who missed both 2026 Nations League windows, while influential defender Daniel Ballard featured only in the first game in Georgia before a hamstring injury.

Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill was forced to pull out of the November squad through injury at a time when he would perhaps have been the most natural replacement for Jamie Donley after the striker picked up a second booking against Ukraine last week and had to miss the finale through suspension.

Having taken over an ageing squad four years ago, O'Neill has rebuilt his playing panel with a group that feels as if it is getting deeper with each international window.

"The encouraging thing is we have players on the outside - we've Bradley to come back in, Ballard to come back in, Ali McCann, young Ceadach, Eoin Toal," added the former Stoke City and Blackburn Rovers boss.

"We have good competition for places now. We're going to need that competition, and some players are going to miss out, but we are building depth to the squad that will help us going forward."

Come the next Nations League, that will be all the way into the uncharted territory of the top tier.

#799. Why Leonardo DiCaprio Didn’t Return for Brad Pitt’s Cliff Booth Movie

Brad Pitt shared the real reason why his Once Upon a Time in Hollywood costar Leonardo DiCaprio isn't in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth: "It just seemed like a big ask."

Leonardo DiCaprio is missing out on The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Though Oscar winner starred in 2019's Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, he opted not to appear in the Quentin Tarantino movie's upcoming sequel due to time constraints, according to his former costar Brad Pitt.

"It would have been great fun, but it required a lot of prosthetics, which is a good couple of weeks prepping to get him," Pitt told The Hollywood Reporter Nov. 16, referencing how the follow-up's trailer teased that DiCaprio's Rick Dalton had become "too fat" for his titular stuntman to serve as a body double. "It’s hardly worth the cost for a cameo."

"It was talked about for a while, but it just seemed like a big ask," the 62-year-old explained, adding that DiCaprio's character does get a few "sweet tributes" in the movie.

But the Titanic alum wasn't the only notable name who declined to return for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. After all, David Fincher stepped in to take the directing reins from Tarantino, who opted to only write the script of the new installment.

"I don’t bemoan that all because it’s such a commitment, especially for a director," Pitt shared. “Things sat around for about nine months and Fincher and I were talking about doing something again, and it just happened."

As for DiCaprio's thoughts on the new movie?

"Ultimately, I cannot wait to see the Cliff Booth story," he told Deadline last year. "I think David Fincher’s the perfect man for the job. Quentin is a huge fan of his work, I’m a huge fan of his work, and there’s nobody better to carry on that lineage and tell that story."

DiCaprio added, "It’s the next phase of Cliff Booth’s life. I’m excited to see it."

#798. On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia

The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds.

When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use.

Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later.

"In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus."

The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO.

During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions.

"One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website.

As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#797. Blake Shelton Shares Best Part of Being Stepdad to Gwen Stefani’s Kids

Blake Shelton revealed what he loves most about being a stepdad to Gwen Stefani's kids Kingston, 20, Zuma, 18, and Apollo, 12, sharing how they spend most afternoons.

Blake Shelton has taken to fatherhood like a honey bee to a honeysuckle.

The “God’s Country” singer shared what one of his favorite parts of parenthood is after becoming stepdad to wife Gwen Stefani’s kids with ex-husband Gavin Rossdale: Kingston, 20, Zuma, 18, and Apollo, 12.

“The most cliche dad thing I do every single day when the kids get home from school, Apollo—our youngest—we throw the football for about 30 minutes,” Shelton told Taste of Country in a clip posted to Instagram Nov. 15. “He’s got this thing, he loves to jump on the trampoline while I throw the football to him, so he can do the crazy Odell Beckham catches, DeAndre Hopkins stuff.”

And while the 50-year-old is happy Apollo is able to get his energy out, Shelton is keeping his feet firmly planted on the ground, quipping, “Just throwing the ball wears me out.”

Thankfully, he and Zuma enjoy a less strenuous activity, as Shelton shared that he and the teen spend time playing the guitar together.

“It’s not me showing him stuff,” the Grammy nominee added. “It's him showing me stuff. ‘Have you heard this song?’ ‘You heard of this artist?’ ‘Listen to this song.’”

The duo share musical moments “almost every single day,” and that along with Apollo’s football antics are just a few of the memories Shelton values as their stepdad.

“I love it,” he said. “I can't wait ’til they get home.”

The “Sangria” singer has also been there to support Stefani’s eldest son Kingston with his musical career, as the couple attended his concert at the Troubadour in Los Angeles Nov. 10, alongside Stefani’s ex Rossdale.

Since tying the knot with Stefani in 2021, Shelton has been candid about how his life has found new fulfillment as a stepdad.

"I didn't know what I was signing up for, but I was all about signing up for it," Shelton said during the 2022 Country Radio Seminar. "And every day I've fallen in love with the boys as much as I do with Gwen."

Sufferin' succotash! The Monstars and Tune Squad interplanetary slam arrived 30 years ago, and it's still a clinic in interplanetary conflict resolution.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.

The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.

In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).

Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.

So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can!

"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.

Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.

While "Independence Day" saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.

Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.

Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs…

Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!

There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.

Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly. "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”

It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.

Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.

MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!

Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.

It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's "Disclosure Day" from a few months ago.

In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.

This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!

"Space Jam" is available to watch on HBO Max.

Chris Brown has made a habit of bringing different women on stage for the “Take You Down” portion of his performance on the R&B Tour, but now he’s entered another age bracket.

C. Breezy had an older woman — who goes by Ms. Joyce — escorted to the stage at Sunday night’s (Nov. 15) show inside Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium, and she was dressed to impress for her moment, which found Ms. Joyce rocking a zebra-print mink coat, a furry hat and shades while walking with a red cane.

Clips quickly made the rounds on social media as CB serenaded Ms. Joyce on a stripper pole and then laid her down and danced on her on a red couch for the top 5 Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart hit, which had Ms. Joyce in a trance and in another dimension mentally.

Brown posted photos from the viral interaction. “Love her,” Breezy captioned the pictures, which Ms. Joyce should have framed and hung up somewhere in her home.

A bunch of the R&B star’s celebrity friends had a laugh at the heartwarming exchange and possible bucket list item for Ms. Joyce. “God bless your heart babe. You gave her a night she will NEVER forget,” actress Taraji P. Henson wrote.

Rapper Ray Vaughn joked, “Life alert bout to go off!” And Lupe Fiasco called the move from Breezy “diabolical.”

With the Nov. 16 date at SoFi Stadium of the R&B Tour canceled, Ms. Joyce will have to travel to get another opportunity to get eye-to-eye with Breezy again.

Next up, the lucrative trek is heading to New Orleans for a pair of shows this weekend before returning to Houston to finish off November. The R&B Tour is currently slated to wrap up in Tampa Bay, Fla., on Dec. 12.

A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth.

NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating."

During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1.

"This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4.

Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2.

A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet.

Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s.

The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did.

Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan, executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane.

Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which manages the mission, is looking to continue to max out the scientific return.

NASA says the mission costs from launch to Neptune, spanning about 12 years from 1977 to 1989, was $865 million — with $30 million more budgeted for its extended mission. "It's a lot of money, right? And it's everyone's money … so we want to make sure that we do it right," Hayes said.

Both nuclear-powered spacecraft are still healthy enough to be chatting with Earth and taking measurements from interstellar space, although dwindling power supplies have forced instrument shutoffs and other creative techniques to be getting the most out of the missions. One example was a huge power swap that took place on both spacecraft this year, called the "Big Bang" because of its impact on the mission.

"It's a balance, right? Because some instruments are more power hungry than others," Hayes said of the ongoing work on keeping the Voyagers going. "Those instruments that use the least amount of power, but give you good science still, they would obviously rise to the top in any sort of priority discussion. Whereas an instrument that is more power-hungry, but still has interesting science, that's on the cusp."

While the two spacecraft are still healthy, Hayes said their age — and the extreme environment they are operating in — makes them "fragile," in his words. "We're way out there. We're a light-day out there, which is just just over 16 billion miles. So it's really really far. It's also really really cold, right? We're only a few degrees above absolute zero here."

The Voyagers continue to lose four watts of power per year (their initial power was at 470 watts apiece) and the challenge is not only the power, but also the propellant. Hydrazine, Hayes said, is prone to freezing. "And if it freezes, then it's game over," he said, paying tribute to the JPL engineers that continue to keep the spacecraft going.

Voyager 1's next destination is vaguely near a star 17 light-years from our planet, in the constellation of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear, or Little Dipper). But the spacecraft will certainly be out of nuclear power by then, as its flyby — at a distance of 1.7 light-years of the star, called Gliese 445 — will take place in 40,000 years.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

"I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet".

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets.

But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic.

"In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule."

As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't."

Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions.

In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome, with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth.

Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility.

Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies. The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart.

"I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022.

The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield.

"It's like Stephen Hawking said, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness."

To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space.

"If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?"

The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords.

Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures.

But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more.

Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them.

"What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose."

To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield.

The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX. It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors.

In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework.

The Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades.

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enforceable, binding options in the future." In the meantime, Jordan-Saifi hopes that players in the space industry will play a role in holding one another accountable to observing the principles of the Astra Carta.

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain, and I don't, frankly, see the big players taking their foot off the gas, both for commercial and for strategic reasons," explained Martinez. "But I think that there is a growing awareness of the fragility of the space domain, and so, therefore, I would expect the major actors to recognise this and to behave responsibly."

Martinez points to SpaceX's Starlink constellation as an example of good behavior on orbit, with the company often sharing satellite trajectories and maneuver plans for other actors to see and plan for ahead of time. "...This is what I think we are all aspiring towards in the future, some form of global, globally coordinated, or global space traffic coordination system. which we don't yet have today."

A heightened risk comes from newcomers drawn to the growing space economy from other sectors. "They don't understand that they're entering a fragile and strategic domain, and that's where initiatives like the Astra Carta can help to socialise this awareness," continued Martinez.

But one of the greatest potential strengths of the Astra Carta may rest with its unique ability to engage the public and raise awareness in the quest for sustainability in space, as much as its capacity to galvanise the private sector.

"The first step is to create social awareness of this, and I would say that one of the values of the Astra Carta is the cachet of royal attention to this issue," said Martinez. "Extending the king's already well known appreciation for stewardship of the Earth environment to the orbital environment. And I think that is the real value of it … if the king is talking about this issue, [it] raises its salience and gets others to think about it."

In this, His Majesty is supported by the SMI and a team of astronaut ambassadors, including Hadfield, U.S. astronaut Nicole Stott and ESA astronaut Tim Peake.

"We're going to Antigua and Barbuda for the heads of government meeting of the Commonwealth, and the king attends that, and we're actually bringing Chris Hadfield on stage to talk to the 2.7 billion citizens of the Commonwealth about the AstraCarta," said Jordan-Saifi touting the SMI's ability to reach a vast global audience. "...We really want more and more people to be involved and be aware about space. And I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet."

However, the sheer scope of the Astra Carta makes it a challenge to communicate to the public. Potential readers may also be surprised to find that the most up-to-date version available on the SMI website is still the "Zero Draft" — the name commonly given to unpolished works not yet ready for publication.

Jordan-Saifi assured me that the Astra Carta's Zero Draft is still relevant and accurate, but that a version 1.0 is currently going through consultation for potential release in the future.

Which begs the question: how would one even gauge the success of so far reaching a roadmap as the Astra Carta? Its voluntary nature makes it inherently challenging, but as Jordan-Saifi notes, there are certain metrics that could be used to indicate how far the Astra Carta has shifted the space economy towards sustainability in the future.

The SMI could track the number of countries and commercial partners that have agreed to adhere to the principles of the Astra Carta, assess public awareness and gauge the success with which its tenants have been formally adopted by the United Nations and other regulatory bodies.

Hadfield, meanwhile, reflected on the difficulties facing the Astra Carta's champions on the long road to sustainability.

"How do you weave in the role of a space agency who has to answer to the national demands and the constraints that they have, both financially and politically?" questioned the former astronaut. "And how do you weave in all of the nonprofits that have all different agendas? The Astra Carta is trying to do all those things, and I think it's done admirably, but it takes patience. And if you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."

Want to know more? Then be sure to head over to the SMI website to read the Astra Carta in full, or you can read a recent op-ed on whether we are currently on track for true space sustainability.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

#783. Carrie Coon Calls for Women to Start Their Own Studio as Elle Women in Hollywood Honorees Push for Change

Coon was honored alongside Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore, Penélope Cruz, Elizabeth Debicki, Rosalind Eleazar, Samantha Morton and Inde Navarrette at the Beverly Hills event.

Some of Hollywood’s biggest stars gathered Monday night for Elle’s annual Women in Hollywood celebration, where the heartfelt speeches toasted women’s achievements while also acknowledging how far the industry still has to go.

This year’s honorees included Carrie Coon, Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore, Penélope Cruz, Elizabeth Debicki, Rosalind Eleazar, Samantha Morton and breakout star Inde Navarrette, who received the Ralph Lauren Spotlight Award.

Pugh, introduced by Dune director Denis Villeneuve, used her speech to thank the women behind the scenes who helped her navigate the industry from a young age. “To be a woman in Hollywood is a bonkers ride,” she said, recognizing the costume designers, makeup artists and crew members whose work often goes unnoticed. Related Stories Movies Joseph Zada Spent a Month Watching "Everything Woody Harrelson Has Ever Done" to Prepare for 'Hunger Games' Role Movies Florence Pugh Celebrates Robert Pattinson's Bond Casting: "He's Been the No. 1 Vote in My Household"

Earlier on the red carpet, Pugh told The Hollywood Reporter that many of those women had looked out for her before she knew how to advocate for herself. “It’s the unseen, it’s the unnoticed work that shapes the women that we grow up to be,” she said.

Coon took a more pointed approach in her speech, questioning the systems that determine whose stories get told and who holds power in Hollywood.

“Patriarchy, capitalism. These are hierarchical systems of domination that rely on fear, and in this paradigm, women and girls, like our natural resources, are a disposable commodity,” she told the room at the Four Seasons Beverly Hills.

Coon pushed back against the idea that women’s stories are interchangeable, drawing on the writings of feminist scholar Bell Hooks to describe how fully inhabiting one’s body through art can itself be an act of resistance. Of her fellow honorees, she said: “I see the fight for the living world. I see moral clarity. I see imagination. I see courage. And these are, in fact, the antidotes to fascism. That’s how important this storytelling is.”

She also challenged the notion that women should have to fight for space in an industry where they remain underrepresented in positions of power.

“As my friend Julianne Moore said recently, we’re 52 percent of the population. That’s not a special interest group,” she said. Rather than simply celebrating women’s achievements for one night, Coon urged the room to consider what they could accomplish together. “I’m going to start with a really stupid question,” she said. “Can we start a studio?!”

Speaking to THR on the red carpet earlier in the evening, Coon had expressed concern about the recent departures of prominent female Hollywood executives and what that could mean for the future of women-led projects.

“When women don’t have greenlight power, then fewer female-led films with either directors or female protagonists get made,” she said. “We’re going to see a drop. We know this. It’s just statistics. It’s just math.”

Cruz also had a few things to say about Hollywood’s treatment of women behind the camera. Reflecting on her experience working with Olivia Wilde on The Invite, she questioned why she’s still asked whether working with a female director feels different. “After 30 years working, when are we gonna get to the day where that is not worth asking anymore?” she questioned.

Moore, meanwhile, thanked Jesse Eisenberg for writing her a leading role in The Debut, a story inspired by his own experiences that he chose to tell through the perspective of a middle-aged woman. “He did what female actors crave. He put me in the center of the narrative,” she said.

There were plenty of laughs throughout the night, too, with introductions from Seth Rogen and Alexander Skarsgård, along with tributes from Daniel Kaluuya and Bryce Dallas Howard. Debicki recalled the casting director who helped launch her career, while Eleazar spoke about her mother, who raised her on her own and shaped her understanding of strength.

Matt Damon paid tribute to Morton, who was unable to attend due to illness. In prepared remarks read on her behalf, Morton spoke about the importance of women supporting one another. “To truly be a woman in Hollywood is not about location, but community,” her statement read.

It was a sentiment that echoed Coon’s earlier call for women to turn the night’s celebration into something more lasting. “Nights like these shouldn’t be one-off nights where we celebrate,” Coon said. “They should be the beginning of those conversations.”

"Sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.

Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

"Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9).

The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated. (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.)

For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated.

The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service.

The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future.

Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur, the successor to the venerable Atlas V.

Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit.

The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef.

Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

“Dance is the hidden language of the soul,” Madonna wrote in a social media post tagging @Grammys, captioned “Incoming love letter.” “When I made Confessions II with Stuart Price, our goal was not just to make people dance, but to find connection with other humans. If Storytelling is how we find our way back to ourselves then dancing is how we get there.

“Thanks to everyone that worked on this record!” the letter continues. “The producers, the writers, the artists and most of all my fans who have been so encouraging and supportive since the beginning of this project. Thank you for sharing this sacred space with me. I’m so grateful to all of you. Love, Madonna.”

The Queen of Pop’s July club album Confessions II received a nomination for best dance/electronic album, best dance/electronic recording for the song “I Feel So Free,” best dance pop recording for “Danceteria” and best remixed recording for the Stuart Price remix of her Kylie Minogue collab “Love Sensation.”

These nominations bring Madonna’s total nominations to 32, with her first coming in 1988. Her seven wins include a few in the dance genre; she got the 1999 best dance recording award for her electronica masterpiece “Ray of Light” and the best dance/electronic album award for her 2007 LP Confessions on a Dancefloor.

Given the warm reception Confessions II has received, there’s reason to believe Madonna could sweep the dance categories at the 2027 ceremony. While the dance categories are typically not televised, the Grammys put one in prime time in 2023, when Beyoncé’s Renaissance was nominated for (and won) best dance/electronic album. Presumably, the Recording Academy may consider this move again given Madonna’s star power.

The 2027 Grammy Awards happen Feb. 7 at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.

The new observatory managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement.

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

#775. These 12 Follow-Ups to Grammy Album of the Year Winners Didn’t Receive a Single Nomination: Full List

Harry Styles is in good company. Such music legends as Carole King, George Harrison and Lionel Richie experienced the same fate.

Harry Styles was doubtless disappointed on Monday (Nov. 16), when Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally., his follow-up to the Grammy album of the year winner Harry’s House, didn’t receive a single Grammy nomination. Styles may take some small comfort in knowing that he’s in good company. Such music legends as Carole King, George Harrison and Lionel Richie experienced the same fate with their follow-ups to Grammy album of the year winners.

Since 1970, 12 follow-ups to Grammy-winning albums have failed to receive a single Grammy nomination. (Before 1970, album release patterns were much different, with artists frequently releasing multiple albums in a year.)

Many of these follow-ups to Grammy-winning albums did well on the Billboard charts. Seven of the 12 (including Styles’ album) topped the Billboard 200. Four of them (again including Styles’ album) both topped the Billboard 200 and spawned at least one single that topped the Billboard Hot 100. One of them – Bee Gees’ Spirits Having Flown topped the Billboard 200 for six weeks and spawned three No. 1 hits.

By definition, Grammy album of the year winners are hard acts to follow. King’s Tapestry, Fleetwood Mac’s Rumours and the Bee Gees-led Saturday Night Fever soundtrack are three of the most iconic and era-defining albums of the 1970s. Any follow-up was probably going to suffer by comparison.

Some of these overlooked follow-ups, notably ’s Fleetwood Mac’sTusk, have risen in esteem over the years.

Here are follow-ups to Grammy-winning albums since 1970 that failed to receive a single Grammy nomination – not for the album or any of its tracks.

Follow-up to: Blood, Sweat & Tears (1970 winner)

Notes: The biggest hit from the album was Carole King and Gerry Goffin’s “Hi-De-Ho,” one of King’s last hits-to-order before she emerged as a superstar in her own right the following year.

Notes: King may have erred in releasing Music so soon after Tapestry – just 10 months later, before Tapestry had even swept the Grammys in March 1972. (Albums were released at a much quicker clip back then.) “Sweet Seasons,” the only single released from Music, cracked the top 10 on the Hot 100. Another song on the album, “It’s Going to Take Some Time,” was a big hit for the Carpenters.

Follow-up to: The Harrison-led, all-star live album The Concert for Bangla Desh (1973 winner)

Notes: This was Harrison’s first studio album since the triple-disk opus All Things Must Pass in 1970. Living in the Material World spawned a No. 1 hit on the Hot 100, “Give Me Love (Give Me Peace on Earth).”

Notes: This double-disk album spawned a pair of top 10 hits on the Hot 100, “Tusk” and “Sara.” That’s just half of the number of top 10 hits that Rumours had produced, but a return to earth was inevitable after an album as colossal as Rumours.

Follow-up to: Bee Gees-led soundtrack Saturday Night Fever (1979 winner)

Notes: This was the brothers’ first studio album since 1976’s Children of the World. “Too Much Heaven,” “Tragedy” and “Love You Inside Out” all reached No. 1 on the Hot 100. If they weren’t quite as epic a three-play as the trio’s Fever singles (“How Deep Is Your Love,” “Stayin’ Alive” and “Night Fever”) had been, they were very good (especially the first two). This album deserved more love than it got at the Grammys.

Follow-up to: Christopher Cross (1981 winner)

Notes: In 1981, Cross became the first artist in Grammy history to sweep each of the “Big Four” Grammy categories – album, record and song of the year plus best new artist. That over-the-top success created a backlash that Cross might have been able to avoid had he just won best new artist. In any event, this album failed to match its predecessor, despite yielding two big hits, the peppy “All Right” and the treacly ballad “Think of Laura.”

Notes: Toto IV included such smashes as “Rosanna” (five weeks at No. 2 on the Hot 100) and “Africa” (No. 1). “Stranger in Town,” the biggest hit from this follow-up, topped out at No. 30.

Follow-up to: Can’t Slow Down (1985 winner)

Notes: This was Richie’s third solo album. It included “Say You, Say Me,” which had been released nine months earlier and had topped the Hot 100 and won an Oscar for best original song. The album also spawned two more top 10 hits, “Dancing on the Ceiling” and “Love Will Conquer All.” After Dancing on the Ceiling, Richie didn’t release another studio album for nearly 10 years.

Follow-up to: Two Against Nature (2001 winner)

Notes: Everything Must Go was the duo’s ninth and final studio album.

Follow-up to: Taking the Long Way (2007 winner)

Notes: Grammy voters were making a statement in voting for Taking the Long Way – actually, several statements. They were standing up for freedom of speech and venting their anger at President George W. Bush and the Iraq war. That angst had died down by the time this long-awaited album was released than 13 years later.

Notes: “Believe” was the only Hot 100 hit from the album, reaching No. 31.

Follow-up to: Harry’s House (2023 winner)

Notes: “Aperture” reached No. 1 on the Hot 100. “American Girls” came close, peaking at No. 4.
