#717. Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin

A badly distorted British silver coin dating to 1834 may hold evidence of an unusual accident during the minting process nearly 200 years ago. New scientific analysis suggests that the remarkable damage to the coin was more likely caused by a manufacturing problem than by ordinary wear, corrosion, or a later impact.

The findings, reported by IA STUDIO in the journal npj Heritage Science, center on a silver sixpence issued during the reign of King William IV. The coin was found in an album containing various coins at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, England. Although the sixpence had an individual price tag of £8, the entire album was subsequently purchased as a single lot rather than the coin being bought separately.

What makes this particular sixpence remarkable is the extent and unusual pattern of its damage. Its central surface appears severely crushed and distorted, yet much of the outer rim and the small grooves along its edge remain relatively intact. The contrast raised an intriguing question about what could have happened to the coin.

To investigate, researchers examined the silver piece using powerful microscopes, chemical testing, and detailed three-dimensional surface measurements. The results point toward an unusual sequence of intense compression, potentially while the coin was being struck at the mint.

A Crushed Silver Coin Reveals Unusual Clues

The most striking evidence came from the coin's severely distorted central regions. Detailed measurements revealed deep, sharply defined depressions, elevated ridges, stepped surfaces, and areas where the metal appeared to have been pushed and displaced in overlapping patterns.

These features were particularly pronounced on the front of the coin, known as the obverse, which bears the portrait of William IV. Across the damaged central portrait area, the difference between the highest and lowest measured points reached approximately 0.75 millimeters.

That may sound small, but it represents a substantial distortion on the surface of a thin silver coin.

The investigators found that the overall damage was most consistent with repeated applications of high pressure concentrated in a limited area. The metal also appears to have been at least partly prevented from spreading outward as the force was applied.

This combination of heavy central damage and relatively well-preserved edges is difficult to reconcile with the gradual effects of circulation or simple corrosion. It also makes a single later impact, with the metal free to move outward, a less convincing explanation.

Instead, the findings favor an unusual problem during the original striking process, although the available evidence does not establish the exact sequence of events with certainty.

Microscopic Analysis Reveals Damage Beneath the Surface

To better understand the unusual deformation, the investigation combined scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) and optical surface profilometry.

The microscopic and chemical examinations provided information about the coin's metal composition and the changes affecting its surface.

In areas that had escaped the worst damage, testing identified an underlying silver and copper alloy. The more severely distorted regions contained lower measured concentrations of silver, higher levels of copper, and additional chemical evidence associated with corrosion and contamination.

These substances were especially concentrated inside the depressions formed by the damaged metal.

However, the chemical results largely reflected changes at the surface. Although corrosion and contamination had affected the coin, they could not adequately account for the depth, shape, and distribution of its unusual distortions.

The team also used optical surface profilometry, a technique that maps the height and shape of a surface in three dimensions. This made it possible to examine the coin's damaged areas in much greater detail than ordinary photographs could provide.

The resulting maps showed steep depressions, raised shoulders, abrupt changes in surface height, and multiple layers of metal displacement.

Using height measurements supplied by the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service, the study's author determined that the damaged central portrait region varied in height by approximately 750 micrometers, equivalent to 0.75 millimeters.

Taken together, the findings suggest that the coin underwent repeated compression while its sideways movement was at least partly restricted. This explanation fits the evidence better than ordinary wear, which generally smooths a coin's surface over time, or corrosion, which tends to remove or chemically alter material.

A Rare Glimpse Into 19th-Century Coin Production

The sixpence was produced in 1834, when Britain was already using steam-powered presses to manufacture coins.

During this period, coins with serious striking defects were typically identified through mint inspections and melted down so the metal could be reused. This was especially important for coins made from precious metals such as silver.

If the unusual deformation occurred during the original minting process, the sixpence may therefore represent a rare surviving example of a manufacturing failure that would ordinarily have been removed from circulation before it ever reached the public.

Such a coin could provide a physical record of a brief mechanical problem during the early era of mechanized coin production.

Determining whether the damage actually occurred at the mint is challenging, however. Historic metal objects can undergo many changes over decades or centuries, and severe deformation may obscure the physical clues needed to identify its origin.

To address this uncertainty, the study examined several kinds of evidence independently. The researchers considered the composition of the underlying metal, chemical changes at the surface, and the three-dimensional geometry of the deformation before comparing the results with different possible explanations.

The findings also demonstrate how non-destructive scientific techniques can be used to investigate other historic metal objects. By combining chemical and structural evidence, researchers may be able to distinguish manufacturing defects from later damage even when visual inspection alone provides no clear answer.

How AI Helped Investigate the Coin Mystery

The investigation also explored how computational tools, including artificial intelligence, could assist in evaluating a historical mystery without replacing physical scientific evidence.

Before any laboratory results were available, the author began by studying high-resolution photographs of the sixpence and systematically reviewing its unusual surface features.

This early examination helped identify several possible causes of the damage and establish what kinds of physical measurements would be needed to test them.

Human-supervised computational tools, including large language models (LLMs), helped organize the observations, develop alternative explanations, compare competing ideas, and formulate questions that could later be investigated through laboratory testing.

Importantly, the initial hypotheses and analytical notes were recorded before the independently produced laboratory measurements became available.

The possible explanations included ordinary circulation wear and corrosion, mechanical damage occurring after minting, later compression under restricted conditions, and deformation during the original manufacturing process.

To investigate these possibilities, independent measurements were commissioned from the Experimental Techniques Centre at Brunel University of London and the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service within the Department of Materials at the University of Oxford.

Once the testing was completed, computational tools were used again to help organize the resulting data and compare the physical findings with the earlier explanations.

"The important sequence was hypothesis first, independent laboratory measurement second," said A. Ikraam, founder of IA STUDIO and author of the study.

"We used the models to ask what features mattered and what evidence could distinguish one explanation from another. Then the laboratory measurements gave us something physical to test those ideas against. The models could support the reasoning process, but they could not decide what happened to the coin."

Scientific Evidence Points to a Possible Minting Error

Although artificial intelligence played a supporting role in organizing observations and evaluating competing possibilities, it did not produce the laboratory measurements or determine the final findings.

The study's conclusions were based on independently generated scientific data, with the author retaining responsibility for interpreting the evidence and deciding which explanation was best supported.

The results favor a rare minting anomaly involving repeated, highly concentrated pressure, rather than damage caused by ordinary circulation, corrosion, or a single unrestricted impact after production. Nevertheless, the research does not conclusively establish every detail of what happened to the sixpence.

Beyond shedding light on the possible origins of a strangely mangled 1834 coin, the investigation illustrates how modern imaging, chemical analysis, and carefully evaluated computational tools can work together to uncover clues hidden in historic objects.

What initially appeared to be little more than a badly damaged silver coin may instead preserve an unusual record of how something went wrong during the early days of mechanized coin manufacturing.

#715. Jeff Bezos Was ‘Heavily Involved’ in Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond and Admits Initial Fears ‘Because He’s Already So Famous’

Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos revealed during a recent appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event that he was “heavily involved” in Amazon MGM casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Bezos said that because Bond is traditionally a star-making role, they were at first “slightly biased” against casting Pattinson because he’s already “so famous.” However, after narrowing down the candidates to five and conducting screen tests, he was the “obvious” choice. Related Stories Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA to Headline Coachella 2027

“We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday,” Bezos said. “There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists. It was interesting. Full costumes and real sets and other actors with them. We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.”

He continued, “By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance. It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob. Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he’s already so famous, like maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

Amazon MGM announced Pattinson as the next James Bond on Monday, ending weeks of rabid media speculation. “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” the “Batman” and “Primetime” star said in a statement after the news broke. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

While Bezos never mentioned them by name, industry analysts seemingly had a handle on the Bond finalists heading into the last weekend of casting. The shortlist of top choices included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult. Other names rumored to be in the running at one include Jacob Elordi, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and even Harry Styles.

Amazon finalized its deal for MGM, the studio behind James Bond, in 2022. However, it didn’t have creative control of the franchise until it bought out longtime Bond producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli for $20 million. Denis Villeneuve and Pattinson’s film will be the first released after the deal.

#714. NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation

After spending more than a year experiencing what life could be like on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally stepped outside, marking the end of an ambitious experiment designed to prepare humans for future missions to the Red Planet.

The crew completed their simulated Mars journey on October 31, 2026, emerging into the outside world for the first time in more than a year. Although the volunteers never actually left Earth, their extended mission recreated many of the challenges astronauts could encounter while living and working millions of miles from home.

The experiment was part of NASA's Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) program, which investigates how people adapt to the demanding conditions of extended space exploration.

The four volunteers were Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right). Following the completion of their mission, the crew posed together outdoors, celebrating their return from a simulated journey to another planet.

Throughout the experiment, the participants carried out tasks similar to those that future Mars explorers may need to perform. These included operating and testing essential systems, caring for crops, conserving limited supplies, and conducting extravehicular activities.

Extravehicular activities, often called spacewalks, are operations astronauts perform outside their spacecraft or habitat. In a Mars simulation, these activities help researchers examine how crews might prepare for and carry out work beyond the safety of their living quarters.

The volunteers also had to manage communication delays, an important challenge for anyone traveling to Mars. Unlike astronauts aboard the International Space Station, who can communicate with Earth almost instantly, future Mars explorers will experience significant delays because radio signals take time to cross the enormous distance between the two planets.

These delays mean astronauts cannot always depend on immediate guidance from mission control. They must be prepared to solve problems, make decisions, and manage unexpected situations with greater independence.

One of the biggest challenges of sending people to Mars is keeping them healthy, productive, and safe during long periods away from Earth. A crew must be able to manage food, equipment, living conditions, and daily responsibilities while working together in a confined environment.

NASA uses analog missions to explore these challenges before attempting actual journeys into deep space. An analog mission is a realistic simulation that reproduces selected conditions of space exploration while allowing scientists to study how people respond in a controlled setting on Earth.

The CHAPEA program provides an opportunity to investigate how astronauts might handle the practical demands of extended missions, including resource limitations, equipment maintenance, food production, and communication difficulties.

The lessons learned from Montgomery, Spicer, Elder, and Ellis will help NASA plan future human exploration missions. Their experiences are expected to inform the development of NASA's planned Moon Base and preparations for eventual crewed expeditions to Mars.

Although this crew's journey took place entirely on Earth, the knowledge gained could help address some of the challenges humans will face when they finally travel to the Red Planet.

"Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update.

The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.

The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)

That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.)

NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. #711. Netflix Eyes Return to Cannes After 10 Years as Festival Lobbies for Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ Starring Josh O’Connor

The streamer hasn't debuted a film at the festival since 2017.

The ice appears to be thawing between Netflix and Cannes.

The streamer, which hasn’t debuted a film at the festival in almost a decade due to France’s strict rules around theatrical releases, is eyeing a return to the south of France in 2027, Variety has learned. Ted Sarandos suggested as much earlier this year, when he told Variety he hoped to “do something special” for Cannes’ 80th edition. Related Stories Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA to Headline Coachella 2027

Now it turns out that Cannes boss Thierry Frémaux has also been making a push to bring Joel Coen’s “Jack of Spades” to the festival for more than a year, sources say. Netflix declined to comment.

The American gothic mystery, starring Josh O’Connor, Patsy Ferran, Frances McDormand, Lesley Manville and Damian Lewis, was at one point expected to be ready for this year’s Cannes, then Venice, but is now on track for next May. Coen also has a strong relationship with Frémaux, who honored him alongside his brother Ethan at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival.

But there’s a catch. Netflix recently acquired “Jack of Spades,” complicating plans for what would otherwise have been a natural Cannes contender.

That means the only way for Netflix to return to Cannes with “Jack of Spades” would be out of competition, which has been a deal-breaker for Sarandos. Sources say Frémaux has been trying to convince Netflix and Sarandos that an out-of-competition premiere can be just as prestigious as a competition slot, pointing to the recent examples of Martin Scorsese’s Apple-backed “Killers of the Flower Moon” and Tom Cruise’s “Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning,” both of which made a major splash on the Croisette without competing for the Palme d’Or.

But recent changes could help smooth the path towards a Netflix comeback on the Croisette. The streamer’s newly-appointed chief content officer Peter Rice is a longtime friend of Cannes who has known Frémaux since his days at Searchlight. His arrival could help bring the two sides closer after years of tensions over theatrical releases.

Netflix may also have good reason to seek a return to Cannes. After losing a few big-name filmmakers, the streamer could be looking to ramp up its prestige profile. While it has increasingly turned to Venice to launch major awards contenders, including Guillermo del Toro’s “Frankenstein” and Noah Baumbach’s “Jay Kelly,” Cannes remains the world’s biggest film festival and arguably the most powerful platform for launching auteur-driven movies.

Netflix knows that better than most. Despite not bringing its own movies to the festival in 10 years, it has snapped up several on the ground there. In 2024, it bought Jacques Audiard’s “Emilia Pérez” which went on earn 13 Oscar nominations and win two Oscars, including best actress for Zoe Saldana. This year, it acquired “La Bola Negra,” now its main hope for awards season — with many tipping it for best picture.

“Jack of Spades” would seem a perfect fit for the festival, where Joel Coen is one of its favorite auteurs. Alongside his brother Ethan, the director has brought films including “Barton Fink,” which won the Palme d’Or and best director awards, “No Country for Old Men” and “Inside Llewyn Davis.”

Netflix hasn’t taken a film to Cannes since 2017, when it premiered both Bong Joon-ho’s “Okja” and Noah Baumbach’s “The Meyerowitz Stories.” It sparked an outcry from French exhibitors, prompting the festival to change its rules the following year to require competition films to receive theatrical releases in France.

The streamer has, however, softened its stance on theatrical releases considerably. “La Bola Negra” is in the middle of a 46-day theatrical rollout, the longest Netflix has given any of its films to date. Next year, “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” will have an exclusive theatrical run, as will Taika Waititi’s animated take on Roald Dahl, “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory.”

#710. 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian

A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that lived entirely in the ocean, something no amphibian alive today is known to do. The unusual animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.

The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period.

Both fossils were uncovered in China's Guizhou Province, in a region that was once submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses.

"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."

The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt.

Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability.

A Giant Armored Amphibian Built for the Seafloor

Because the two skeletons are so complete, researchers were able to piece together the animal's appearance and develop a clearer picture of how it lived.

Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form.

Its body was also covered in thick bony armor, which may have helped protect it from large marine predators such as ichthyosaurs.

"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."

The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach.

"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.

How Could an Amphibian Survive in Salt Water?

One of the biggest mysteries surrounding Gerrothorax maritimus is how it managed to survive in an environment that is hostile to nearly all modern amphibians.

The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water.

"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."

As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. Even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover.

The ancient Gerrothorax maritimus, however, may have evolved a very different solution.

Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.

Under this proposed mechanism, water would have been absorbed through the digestive tract, while the animal's gills could have helped eliminate excess salt. Gills are known to have been present in members of the Gerrothorax genus, giving the researchers reason to suspect that this species possessed a more fishlike approach to managing its salt balance.

Together, these adaptations may explain how an amphibian managed to occupy an ecological niche that remains inaccessible to its modern relatives.

Fossil Evidence Points to a Fully Marine Lifestyle

The researchers also examined whether Gerrothorax maritimus truly lived in the ocean or whether its remains might have been transported there after death.

Several clues strongly favor a marine lifestyle.

First, the skeletons were recovered from sediments deposited in a deep marine environment. Their remarkable completeness also provides important evidence about where the animals died.

"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."

The preservation of such delicate skeletal structures suggests that the bodies were not carried long distances before reaching the seafloor.

To investigate further, the team analyzed the fossils' chemical composition, focusing on the relative abundance of different forms of strontium, known as isotopes.

The results closely matched the strontium isotope signatures expected in ocean water during the Late Triassic, providing another independent line of evidence that the animals inhabited a marine environment.

Taken together, the fossil preservation, geological setting, and chemical findings make a compelling case that Gerrothorax maritimus spent its life entirely at sea.

The discovery reveals an unexpected evolutionary path for amphibians, showing that at least one ancient species appears to have overcome the biological limitations that keep its living relatives largely confined to freshwater environments.

The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.

Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.

However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.

The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.

"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.

Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.

This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

#707. NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields

Turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans. But turbulence also occurs throughout space, where it behaves in ways that scientists are still struggling to understand.

Unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state). These particles interact strongly with magnetic and electric fields, creating turbulence that is fundamentally different from what we experience on Earth. Space plasma is also so thinly spread that particles rarely collide with one another, making its behavior even more unusual.

Scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations. Now, an international research team has uncovered a surprising clue: hidden within the seemingly random motion of space plasma is a distinct magnetic pattern that reverses direction at very small scales.

The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, reveals a previously unobserved phenomenon that could improve our understanding of the solar wind and the turbulent conditions that influence space weather.

NASA's Parker Solar Probe Reveals a Hidden Magnetic Reversal

Researchers from the Technische Universität Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, working with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other international institutions, identified the phenomenon using observations from NASA's Parker Solar Probe.

The collaboration brought together scientists from ten countries, including researchers at the Institute of Theoretical Physics at Technische Universität Braunschweig.

By analyzing highly precise measurements of magnetic fields and particles, the team discovered that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at a particular range of wavelengths. This marks the first direct observation of such a reversal in space turbulence.

Even more surprisingly, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths as the solar wind travels farther from the Sun.

The change occurs at a critical boundary where the behavior of plasma shifts from the collective movement of a flowing fluid to the dynamics of individual particles. This connection suggests that the magnetic reversal may provide an important new way to understand how turbulence operates across different physical scales.

Finding Order in the Chaos of Space Turbulence

At larger scales, plasma moves much like a fluid. Swirling structures called vortices and electromagnetic waves create increasingly complex fluctuations, producing the turbulent conditions found throughout space.

Although these movements appear random, the researchers discovered that the rotation of the magnetic fields follows a consistent pattern.

When viewed along a direction pointing outward from the Sun, magnetic fields at larger scales tend to rotate counterclockwise. At much smaller scales, however, the preferred rotation switches to clockwise.

This reversal occurs precisely where plasma stops behaving primarily like a fluid and begins exhibiting behavior governed by individual particles.

The finding is particularly striking because it reveals a clear, organized feature within a system otherwise dominated by seemingly unpredictable fluctuations.

"We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions," says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa (TU Braunschweig), the study's first author.

Dr. Yokoi (University. of Tokyo) emphasizes the broader importance of the discovery, stating, "The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics."

Why the Discovery Matters for Solar Storms and Space Weather

Although the magnetic reversal occurs at extremely small scales, understanding it could have far-reaching consequences for space physics.

Plasma turbulence is a major feature of many environments throughout the universe, including Earth's magnetosphere, the solar wind, regions affected by solar eruptions, interplanetary space, and the disks of material surrounding astronomical objects known as accretion disks.

It also influences the shock waves and clouds of magnetic material that travel through interplanetary space following eruptions on the Sun.

These disturbances can play an important role in geomagnetic storms, making plasma turbulence a critical factor in efforts to predict space weather.

By showing how an organized magnetic pattern emerges as turbulent plasma transitions from fluid behavior to particle behavior, the new research provides an important piece of a longstanding physics puzzle. The findings could ultimately help scientists better understand the complex processes that govern the solar wind and improve the physical models used to forecast geomagnetic storms.

Thomas Velde, who served as head film buyer at AMC Theatres during his 27 years at the exhibitor, died Oct. 31. He was 83.

Velde died of cancer at his home in Rancho Mirage, Calif..

For 27 years, he worked at AMC Theatres, where he negotiated film agreements with domestic and international studios while also overseeing the entertainment company’s Canadian operations and real estate ventures. Following his time at AMC, he worked independently in motion picture distribution and would consult for clients that included Microspace Communications and CJ America. A celebration of life will be held Dec. 8 at 3 p.m. at Woodland Hills Community Church. Donations can be made to the Will Rogers Motion Picture Pioneers Foundation or the Motion Picture and Television Fund, both of which serve the industry community Velde was a part of.

#705. The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a new placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. New placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

Chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

"Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals."

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

The results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

These findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals."

We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City."

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!"

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Travelling outside the US and still want access to Neuromancer? Good news: NordVPN can help you get around those pesky geo-blocking restrictions so you can watch the streaming service you've paid for anywhere in the world.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

Molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

Molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel."

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer’s" eclectic cast is a mix of fresh faces and wily veterans that includes:

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

It’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard announced last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”

#702. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an important role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

Cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

These plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form quickly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol."

To investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

All three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

The researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

While genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks

The new investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

One of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns showed substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

The researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

LDL showed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an important distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," says Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future."

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

All three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

By identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers new possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

"Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments."

The results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

At the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

#700. Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago

An ancient rodent of extraordinary size has been identified from fossils uncovered in a mine in southern Thailand. The discovery, made by an international team of paleontologists that includes scientists from McGill University, provides new evidence that giant rodents appeared much earlier and in more parts of the world than previously believed.

The researchers found "remarkably large" fossilized teeth belonging to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae. This prehistoric rodent lived approximately 34 million years ago, during the middle of the Paleogene period. Its remains, consisting of a lower second molar and a lower incisor, were recovered from the Bang Mark Pit at the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand's Krabi Province.

Although only two teeth have been identified, they offer valuable clues about rodent gigantism, the evolutionary process through which rodents develop unusually large bodies. The discovery suggests that Southeast Asia played a more significant role in the early evolution of giant rodents than scientists had recognized.

Giant Rodents Have a Much Older History Than Expected

"Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems," said Virginie Millien, a biology professor at McGill University and co-author of the study. "Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an important role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents."

The newly identified animal's name reflects both its impressive size and its connection to Thailand. Yakamys combines "yak," the Thai word for giant, with "mys," the Greek word for mouse or rat.

The second part of its scientific name recognizes an important supporter of scientific research in Thailand.

"The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand," Millien said.

How Big Was This 34-Million-Year-Old Rodent?

To estimate the animal's size, the research team applied seven established methods that use tooth measurements to calculate body mass. Their results suggest that Yakamys sirindhornae weighed approximately 30 kilograms, making it about twice as heavy as other known rodents from the same period, including Hulgana.

That would have made the newly discovered species exceptionally large compared with its contemporaries. However, the researchers emphasize that determining an extinct animal's weight from a small number of fossilized teeth involves considerable uncertainty.

"This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation," Millien said.

The limited fossil evidence also makes it difficult to reconstruct how Yakamys evolved or what its life was like. Additional discoveries will be needed to better understand its physical characteristics, ecological role, and evolutionary relationships.

International Research Uncovers Thailand's Prehistoric Past

The fossils were identified through an ongoing international collaboration investigating ancient mammals in Thailand's Krabi Basin. The project brings together scientists from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, and French research organizations, including CNRS and Université de Poitiers.

By revealing evidence of an unusually large rodent in Southeast Asia 34 million years ago, the discovery expands scientists' understanding of where and when rodent gigantism emerged. Future fossil finds could help establish how these ancient giants lived and how their evolution relates to the enormous rodents that appeared elsewhere in the world.

The research received support from CNRS, Université de Poitiers, Université de Montpellier, McGill University, and the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.

Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit.

Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years.

Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.

London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite, at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles).

The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent.

The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft.

The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit.

Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit.

"Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks."

Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the company has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding.

Foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris removal, satellite servicing or debris tracking that have raised funds in 2026. Others include Starfish Space (which raised more than $100 million in a Series B), Katalyst Space ($12 million in funding) and international companies like India's Cosmoserve Space.

Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.
